title: The Dragon Who Sang to the Stars
markdown:
The Sun-Kissed Peaks of Aeridor scraped sky and wore cloud like old shawls. Rope ferries danced between the giants, bells making a thin melody on mist. It was a place that made a person feel correctly small. This year the Sky-Shimmer Festival wanted aerial daring and joyous shouts echoing peak to peak, and they had asked Witch Juniper to judge, which said more about the committee than about Juniper. Practicality was her style, not fanfare. Riddle the jackdaw rode her shoulder, obsidian-eyed, a specialist in the unusual honed by years of looking down on people who thought they were looking up.

“Judging a Festival of Flurry and Flair,” Riddle croaked, dry as skittering leaves.

Juniper settled spectacles that lived dangerously on her nose. “Acrobatics. Loud delight. Straightforward. A tad bewildering.” The cloak was sensible grey. Fanfare was other people’s hobby.

The festival opened not with a bang but with banners unfurling down sheer faces, billowing, catching sun like a thousand captured rainbows. Merchants haggled over woven cloud-silk and sun-gem trinkets in a market that hung impossibly in thin air, tethered by rope and audacity. Voices, coin, crackle. And still Juniper sensed a hollowness. The cheers had rehearsal in them, performance rather than delight. Riddle’s weight on her shoulder was the usual comfort, and then his beak found her ear. Riddle’s beak found her ear. “There.” A far peak, summit in mist, and Ignis the Great hunched as if the sky had cancelled him. Stories whispered that his scales were polished obsidian catching starlight. He was not roaring, not breathing anything impressive. His colossal form slumped against the sky like a fallen titan, a shadow of sorrow on a bright canvas.

“Deflated,” Juniper said. “For a dragon meant to awe, he is remarkably sad.”

“Dragons,” Riddle sighed, quoting a hermit, “arrive as if invited by the weather.” This one looked uninvited to his own party.

Fairness, in Juniper, was a breeze that did not ask permission. She was not given to leaving magnificent creatures to suffer in decorative silence. A self-propelled gust, smelling faintly of lavender and old parchment, lifted her and Riddle toward the lonely perch. The sheer scale of Ignis arrived late, the way mountains do: a wingspan that could eclipse a village, a shadow to make a storm cloud envious. Yet those eyes, large as carriage wheels, usually sold as molten gold, seemed rimmed with something uncomfortably like tears. A dragon crying. Juniper’s curiosity sat up and refused to lie down.

“Greetings, Great Ignis. Juniper. Festival judge. You seem troubled.”

The rumble vibrated in Juniper’s bones, old as the range, more sigh than roar. “Troubled. My spirit is frost on a pane. These contests are loud. Sharp movements, sudden roars. They demand impressiveness: the most dazzling raw power, the most ear-splitting shriek.” He shifted; stone groaned. “My heart keeps the quiet rhythm of ancient rock. My fire is not for scorching sky. It warms the deepest caverns. My artistry is the subtle shift of a mountain’s shadow, wind through pine. This flurry and flair mocks my soul. It makes me a clumsy oaf at a delicate ballet.”

Juniper fitted the pieces. Artist, not battering ram. Delicate feelings, currently being used as a drum.

“The festival’s idea of impressive is narrow. Perhaps a category for emotional resonance.”

Riddle brightened. “Bonus points for a profound crisis?”

She nudged him. “Something visible. Ignis: not might. Sensitivity. Connection. Quiet beauty.”

“They want noise. I am too subtle for their ears.”

“They want last year’s gift. Show this year’s. Sculpt moonlight. Paint mist. Sing sleeping stone. Gentleness is not a defect.”

With Juniper’s guidance and Riddle’s chirps — “Poetry in a puff of smoke” — Ignis prepared without gathering speed, without practising a roar. He sat. He breathed luminous smoke that coalesced into shimmering ephemeral sculptures, starlight on a short lease. He hummed a low resonant tune that made air thrum with a peace you felt in the skeleton. He showed how sunset on his scales did not merely gleam but pulsed with the colours of a thousand blooming flowers, a living tapestry that had not asked to compete.

Therefore, when his turn came, the roaring and flashing of contestants who had been escalating ferocity died back. A hush fell over the archipelago, canyon-deep. Juniper, grey cloak a grounding full stop, simply gestured.

Ignis exhaled a stream of pure soft light that drifted up, tracing patterns on twilight. Not a blast. A gentle aurora, a painted sky of dreams, evolving with irritating grace. Then the low melodic hum wrapped the valley, soothing frayed nerves, making even professional shouters pause and feel something uncontracted: quiet wonder, the sense of a familiar blanket. The crowd, booked for fury, found itself captivated by tender work. Banners learned a newer, more elegant dance. Bells, usually boisterous, chimed softer, as if embarrassed by their own boom.

The reversal was a collective, awestruck sigh, not a bang. The most impressive dragon, booked as catastrophe, had shown that awe could live in quiet beauty and a feeling that did not shatter rock. Villagers trained on constant spectacle found themselves enchanted by a creature who poured his heart into the sky and looked, for a change, like an artist instead of a weather event.

Juniper and Riddle watched the glow hold. She did not announce a moral about softness. Riddle’s eyes took the luminous work and, for once, did not add a joke. They started down while the song was still finding the pine needles, and the festival, having met a quieter kind of shine, had the sense not to cheer it off the mountain.
characters: Juniper (sharp-eyed witch in a sensible grey cloak), Riddle (a jackdaw whose obsidian eyes miss nothing)
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for teens
